title: Cold or warm
hookLine: whether you're cold or warm, sleepy or rested, do your duty (Meditations 6.2)
carry: nobody claps, the work is good anyway

cards: Three in the morning. The baby is crying again, and it's your turn. Or the alarm goes off for the early shift and the room is freezing.
Or you promised to help a friend move, and you slept four hours. It's easy to keep a list of conditions for doing a thing well: warm, rested, appreciated, in the mood.
Book six of the Meditations opens, and its second entry crosses that whole list out.

teach.h: COLD OR WARM, DO YOUR DUTY.
teach.b: In George Long's translation, Meditations six, two begins: "Let it make no difference to thee whether thou art cold or warm, if thou art doing thy duty." Then Marcus keeps going, pair by pair. Drowsy or rested.
Spoken badly of or praised. Even dying or doing something else.
Each pair is a condition we use as an excuse. I'll be patient when I've slept. I'll be generous when people notice.
Marcus treats them all as weather: real, uncomfortable, and not in charge. Then the surprise at the end.

teach.h: EVEN DYING IS AN ACT OF LIFE.
teach.b: He says dying is one of the acts of life too, and in that act, as in any other, it's enough to do well the thing in hand. He doesn't make death a special exam.
It's one more task, done as well as you can on the day it comes.
What he isn't saying: ignore your body, or never rest. Elsewhere he admits that staying under the covers feels more pleasant. The point is narrower.
When the duty is actually yours, right now, the shivering isn't a reason to do it badly. And there's a quiet dignity in work done well while tired.
A nurse at the end of a double shift. A parent at three in the morning. Nobody claps.

how: Readers of Marcus often use 'cold or warm' as a private reminder when they're tired or unappreciated, to do the task in front of them as well as they would on a good day.

games.q: it's freezing, you slept badly, and the duty in front of you is really yours. what does Marcus say?
o: do it, and do it well, cold or warm.
games.why: Meditations 6.2: let it make no difference whether you're cold or warm, drowsy or rested, if you're doing your duty.

practice: Notice whatever discomfort you have right now, tired eyes, a stiff back, a cold hand, and name it plainly without fighting it.
Then picture one duty waiting for you, dishes, a call, a bedtime story, done today as you are, and done well.

wordCard.voice: George Long, whose translation has Marcus write: let it make no difference whether you are cold or warm, if you are doing your duty. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, 'the fitting thing': what Marcus says to do, cold or warm, in 6.2; Long renders it 'thy duty'.

carryVoice: Your line: nobody claps, the work is good anyway. Cold or warm, it's only weather. That's day five hundred seventy-three.
